clinicalPearls: Acute rheumatic fever is a delayed immune-mediated sequela of group A streptococcal pharyngitis, typically emerging a few weeks after the sore throat, and is a diagnosis of the whole child rather than any single test.
Diagnosis rests on the revised Jones criteria, which now stratify populations into low-risk and moderate-to-high-risk to improve sensitivity where the disease remains endemic.
Migratory polyarthritis of the large joints is the commonest major manifestation and is characteristically exquisitely responsive to salicylates.
Carditis is the only manifestation that causes long-term morbidity; a pancarditis, its hallmark is valvulitis with the mitral valve most often affected, followed by the aortic valve.
Sydenham chorea may appear in isolation and late, after other manifestations have resolved, and can be the sole criterion sufficient for diagnosis.
Subcutaneous nodules and erythema marginatum are uncommon but highly specific minor major manifestations, nodules correlating with severe carditis.
Evidence of preceding streptococcal infection (rising anti-streptolysin O or anti-DNase B titres, or positive throat culture) is essential except in isolated chorea or indolent carditis.
Secondary prophylaxis with long-acting penicillin is the cornerstone of preventing recurrent attacks and progressive rheumatic heart disease.
reference.pathophysiology: Acute rheumatic fever follows pharyngeal infection with rheumatogenic strains of group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus in a genetically susceptible host. Molecular mimicry between streptococcal antigens, particularly M protein and the group A carbohydrate N-acetyl-glucosamine, and human tissue proteins such as cardiac myosin and laminin drives a cross-reactive humoral and T-cell response. Antibody binding to valvular endothelium up-regulates adhesion molecules, recruiting CD4+ T cells that release inflammatory cytokines and produce the granulomatous Aschoff bodies pathognomonic of rheumatic carditis. The same autoimmune mechanism targets the basal ganglia to produce chorea, the joints to produce arthritis, and the skin. Repeated episodes amplify valvular scarring, leading to chronic rheumatic heart disease.
additionalInvestigations: throat swab culture and rapid antigen testing for group A streptococcus
serial anti-streptolysin O and anti-DNase B titres
electrocardiogram for PR-interval prolongation and conduction disturbance
echocardiography with Doppler to detect subclinical valvulitis
full blood count and blood cultures to exclude sepsis or endocarditis
redFlags: new or changing cardiac murmur with signs of heart failure indicating severe carditis
pericardial rub or effusion suggesting pancarditis
recurrent attack in a child with established rheumatic heart disease
reference.prognosis: Arthritis and chorea resolve without sequelae, but the prognosis is dictated by the severity of carditis, which may progress to chronic rheumatic heart disease. Faithful secondary prophylaxis markedly reduces recurrence and can allow mild valve lesions to regress.
pitfalls: Attributing a febrile arthritis to rheumatic fever without documented antecedent streptococcal infection, especially in low-incidence settings.
Starting salicylates or steroids before the joint picture has declared itself, masking the diagnostic migratory pattern.
Overlooking subclinical carditis detectable only on echocardiography in a child with apparently isolated arthritis.
Failing to institute and sustain secondary prophylaxis, the single most important determinant of long-term outcome.
Misreading isolated late-onset chorea as a functional or psychiatric disorder.
